title: How Claude Desktop stores Code sessions, and how I share them across accounts
summary:
I use Claude Code inside Claude Desktop with two accounts on the same laptop: a personal one and a work one. For a while, one small thing annoyed me every day:

every time I switched accounts, my entire Code sidebar changed.

The session I'd been working in an hour earlier was simply gone until I switched back. Nothing was deleted. It just belonged to the other account.

So I dug into where Claude Desktop keeps those sessions, and wrote a small open-source helper, My Shared Claude, that gives all my accounts one shared local session list. This post covers what I found and how it works.

Not affiliated with Anthropic. This relies on Claude Desktop's current on-disk layout, which could change in any update.

Where the sessions live

Claude Desktop keeps a data folder per user:

OS Data folder
macOS ~/Library/Application Support/Claude
Windows %APPDATA%\Claude (plus some Store-package variants)
Linux ~/.config/Claude

Inside it, local Code sessions are stored like this:

claude-code-sessions/
  /
    /
      local_.json
      local_.json
      ...

Each account/organization pair gets its own folder of local_*.json session records. The Code sidebar only reads the folder that matches whoever is signed in. That's the whole reason sessions "disappear" when you switch.

One surprise: a single email login can have several organization folders, so you'll often find more folders than you have accounts.

The approach: merge once, then link

I considered syncing copies back and forth, but that means watching files, resolving conflicts on every change, and running something in the background. Instead, the tool does a one-time merge and then lets the filesystem do the work:

  1. Find every claude-code-sessions/// folder.
  2. Merge all local_*.json records into one shared store (shared-code-sessions/). If the same session ID appears in two folders, the most recently modified file wins.
  3. Back up each original folder by moving it to a timestamped backup directory.
  4. Link each original folder path to the shared store.

After that, every account reads and writes the same folder, so new sessions show up everywhere automatically. Nothing runs in the background.

def create_directory_link(path, target):
    if sys.platform == 'win32':
        # A junction needs no Developer Mode or admin rights
        ...  # New-Item -ItemType Junction via PowerShell
    else:
        path.symlink_to(target, target_is_directory=True)

Windows: junctions, not symlinks

On macOS and Linux a plain symlink is fine. On Windows, creating a symlink usually needs Developer Mode or admin rights, which I wanted to avoid for non-technical teammates. Directory junctions work for a normal user, so the tool creates those through PowerShell.

Two details mattered:

  • Paths are passed as quoted literals inside an encoded PowerShell command, so a folder name with odd characters stays data and can't become part of the command.
  • Removing a link has to remove the link, not the folder it points to. On Windows a junction is removed with rmdir. The tool refuses to remove anything that isn't actually a link.

Not sharing what shouldn't be shared

Session records contain some fields that belong to the account that created them, such as Remote Control / bridge IDs and remote MCP server configuration. Carrying those into another account would be wrong, so imported copies have them stripped:

def clean(record):
    result = dict(record)
    for key in list(result):
        if key.startswith(('remoteControl', 'bridge', 'steeredByRemote')) or key in {
            'remoteMcpServersConfig', ...
        }:
            result.pop(key, None)
    result['remoteControlAutoEligible'] = False
    return result

What it deliberately doesn't touch:

  • logins and subscriptions
  • ordinary chats, Cowork and cloud sessions
  • connectors and their authentication
  • org policies and available models
  • sidebar preferences (folder grouping is per account)

One honest caveat: only combine histories you're comfortable having available under every included account. If one of them is a work org, think about that first.

Safety rails

Since this moves folders that hold your conversation history, most of the code is about not making things worse:

  • Claude must be closed. It checks for running Claude processes and stops if it finds any.
  • Preview first. The default run is a dry run that reports what it found. Nothing changes until you type SHARE.
  • Validation before touching anything. Every record must be a real file (not a symlink), parse as JSON, and have a sessionId that matches its filename and is a valid UUID. Anything unexpected stops the run before any folder is moved.
  • Journal plus backups. Each change is recorded in a small JSON journal (written atomically, owner-only permissions), so status and undo know exactly what was done.
  • One-step undo. Undo removes the links and restores the original folders from backup. New sessions created while sharing was on stay in the shared store, so nothing is lost.

Making it usable for non-developers

Half the people I wanted to help don't use a terminal, so each OS gets a double-click launcher (.command, .cmd, .sh) that checks for Python 3.9+ and then shows a small menu:

1. Set up / add accounts (default)
2. Check status
3. Undo sharing
4. Exit

There are no dependencies, nothing to pip install, and it never asks for admin rights or sudo.

Testing on three OSes

The filesystem behavior is the risky part, and it differs per OS. GitHub Actions runs the test suite on macOS, Windows and Ubuntu with Python 3.9 and 3.12, covering setup, adding a new account later, and undo using real symlinks and junctions.

I've verified end-to-end history loading in Claude Desktop on macOS. On Windows and Linux, the automated filesystem tests pass, and I'd really like reports from real installs.

Try it

  • Repo (MIT): https://github.com/gtarun/My-Shared-Claude
  • Direct download: https://github.com/gtarun/My-Shared-Claude/releases/latest/download/My-Shared-Claude-v1.0.zip
  • Product Hunt (launched today, feedback welcome): https://www.producthunt.com/products/my-shared-claude

Quit Claude, double-click the launcher for your OS, check the preview, and type SHARE.

If you try it, I'd love to hear:

  1. Does it work on your Windows or Linux setup?
  2. Would you want to choose which accounts get linked, instead of all of them?

title: Get told when a target account starts hiring, from its own career site
summary:
Hiring is one of the clearest public signals of what a company is about to do. Five new account executive roles mean a sales push and a need for sales tooling. A first data engineer means a data stack is being chosen. A senior role that keeps disappearing and coming back means a recruiter's pitch. The signal is in the change, not the job list: a company with 600 open roles tells you little until you know which 40 appeared this week.

This post sets up a daily watch on a list of target accounts and turns the changes into a short list for the account owners.

Disclosure: I'm Aurelix, and I built the Career Page Monitor. It's a paid tool (prices below).

What it remembers between runs

You list companies as domains (stripe.com), careers pages or job-board links. It finds the company's board on Greenhouse, Lever, Ashby, SmartRecruiters, Workable, BambooHR or Workday and remembers every role under a watchlistId. The first run is the baseline; every later run returns:

  • One company_summary row per company: ats, open_roles now and at the previous run, new_roles, removed_roles, reposted_roles, net_change, new_roles_7d and new_roles_30d, a hiring_acceleration flag (after 14 days of tracking), and the top growing departments, locations and seniority levels.
  • One role_change row per new, removed or reposted role (free): event, title, department, seniority, city, country, remote, url.

A role that comes back under a new ID with the same title and location within repostWindowDays (30 by default) is counted as reposted, not as new hiring.

A morning list for the account owners 

pip install apify-client

import os
from collections import defaultdict

from apify_client import ApifyClient

TEAMS_WE_SELL_TO = ("sales", "revenue", "customer success", "go to market")

client = ApifyClient(os.environ["APIFY_TOKEN"])
run = client.actor("aurelix/hiring-signal-monitor").call(
    run_input={
        "companies": ["stripe.com", "ramp.com", "https://jobs.lever.co/spotify",
                      "https://jobs.ashbyhq.com/notion"],
        "watchlistId": "sales-targets",
        "includeRoleEvents": True,
    }
)
rows = list(client.dataset(run["defaultDatasetId"]).iterate_items())

new_in_team = defaultdict(list)
for r in rows:
    if r["record_type"] == "role_change" and r["event"] == "new":
        if any(t in (r["department"] or r["title"]).lower() for t in TEAMS_WE_SELL_TO):
            new_in_team[r["company"]].append(r)

for s in sorted((r for r in rows if r["record_type"] == "company_summary"),
                key=lambda s: s["new_roles_7d"] or 0, reverse=True):
    if s["status"] != "ok" or s["baseline"]:
        print(f"{s['company']}: {s['status']}{' (baseline saved)' if s['baseline'] else ''}")
        continue
    flag = " ACCELERATING" if s["hiring_acceleration"] else ""
    teams = ", ".join(d["name"] for d in s["top_departments_growing"])
    print(f"{s['company']} ({s['ats']}): {s['open_roles']} open, {s['net_change']:+d} since last run, "
          f"{s['new_roles_7d']} new this week{flag}. Growing: {teams}")
    for role in new_in_team[s["company"]][:3]:
        print(f"    new: {role['title']} ({role['city'] or 'no city'}) {role['url']}")

Run it once to save the baseline, then schedule it daily (save the input as a task in the Apify Console and click Schedule). Put a Slack incoming-webhook URL in webhookUrl and each run also posts a ready-made digest of new, reposted and removed roles per company.

How other teams read the same rows:

  • Recruiting agencies: filter role_change rows on event = reposted. A role that keeps coming back is often hard to fill, and title_normalized, city and url give you the exact role to pitch.
  • Investors: run the portfolio weekly with "includeRoleEvents": false for one summary row per company, and copy open_roles, net_change and new_roles_30d into a sheet.
  • Job seekers: the companies you want to work for and a Slack webhook, daily, so a new role reaches you the morning after it opens.

If you want every open role with its full description rather than the changes, the Greenhouse Jobs Scraper returns whole boards, and its board URLs go into companies here unchanged. To watch competitors' jobs alongside their new ads, page edits and prices in one report, there is Competitor Watch.

Why this tool

  • Remembers every role between runs and reports what opened and what closed.
  • Reposted roles are told apart from new hiring.
  • Workday career sites are included.
  • Charged per company checked, whatever the size of its board.
  • What it doesn't cover: job descriptions, salary and the technologies a posting names.

Limits

  • Seven job-board systems only. iCIMS, Taleo, SuccessFactors, Oracle and home-made careers sites are not covered; those companies come back as not_found and are not charged.
  • Detection needs a careers page that links or embeds the board, or a board named like the company. Paste the board link when it fails.
  • Workday shows at most 2,000 jobs per search; larger sites are split by job family or location when Workday allows it, otherwise marked partial. Workday list pages have no department, and Workday removals are reported one run later.
  • Velocity uses the posting date the board publishes, which some employers reset when they refresh postings; BambooHR publishes none.
  • Seniority is inferred from the title and can be wrong for unusual titles.
  • Up to 50 companies per run; use several watchlists for longer lists. Changes are only as fresh as your schedule.

Cost

You pay once per company actually checked in a run, whatever its size and whatever changed; role-change rows are free, and companies whose board could not be found or read are not charged. The current price is on the Store page; Apify's free plan includes $5 of credit a month, about 500 company checks, enough for a daily watch on a dozen accounts.

title: Optimizing Real-Time Computer Vision Inference Pipelines in Python for Edge Monitoring
summary:
The Latency Bottleneck in Edge Vision

Running object detection models like YOLOv8 on edge hardware requires careful memory and frame-rate management. Processing every single frame from a camera stream often saturates the CPU/GPU without adding meaningful diagnostic value—especially when monitoring slow-changing physical environments like plant health or industrial gauges.

In this guide, we will implement a frame-sampling and asynchronous inference wrapper in Python to keep latency low and resource usage predictable.

Designing a Non-Blocking Inference Queue

Instead of running model inference directly inside the camera capture loop, we decouple frame capture from model execution using a bounded queue.Queue of size 1. This ensures the model always evaluates the most recent frame while dropping stale frames automatically.

import threading
import queue
import time

class EdgeInferencePipeline:
    def __init__(self, model, target_fps: float = 2.0):
        self.model = model
        self.interval = 1.0 / target_fps
        self.frame_queue = queue.Queue(maxsize=1)
        self.running = False

    def push_frame(self, frame):
        if self.frame_queue.full():
            try:
                self.frame_queue.get_nowait()
            except queue.Empty:
                pass
        self.frame_queue.put(frame)

    def _worker(self):
        while self.running:
            start_time = time.perf_counter()
            try:
                frame = self.frame_queue.get(timeout=1.0)
                results = self.model.predict(frame, verbose=False)
                self.handle_detections(results)
            except queue.Empty:
                continue

            elapsed = time.perf_counter() - start_time
            sleep_time = max(0.0, self.interval - elapsed)
            time.sleep(sleep_time)

    def handle_detections(self, results):
        for r in results:
            boxes = r.boxes
            print(f"Detected {len(boxes)} objects at {time.strftime('%X')}")

    def start(self):
        self.running = True
        threading.Thread(target=self._worker, daemon=True).start()

    def stop(self):
        self.running = False

Adding Basic Telemetry Metrics

To monitor how healthy our inference service is in production, we should track average inference duration and frame drop rates:

def measure_inference(model, sample_image):
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    _ = model.predict(sample_image, verbose=False)
    latency_ms = (time.perf_counter() - t0) * 1000
    print(f"Inference latency: {latency_ms:.2f} ms")
    return latency_ms

Conclusion

Decoupling frame capture from model inference prevents memory leaks and keeps edge hardware responsive. Combined with lightweight latency logging, you can reliably deploy computer vision models on local hardware without cloud round-trip delays.

title: How R6 Stat Trackers Compute K/D and Win Rate (And Why Two Sites Disagree)
summary:
Stat trackers for Rainbow Six Siege look like simple profile pages: a rank, a K/D, a win rate, maybe a list of operators. Under the hood they have to agree with Ubisoft's ranked data, survive rate limits, handle divide-by-zero, and pick a win-rate denominator that two honest engineers can still argue about.

This post walks through those choices, using how the numbers are calculated on SiegeRadar as a public example. SiegeRadar is a free unofficial tracker, not affiliated with Ubisoft. The same questions show up in any similar app. For the game itself, see Ubisoft's official Rainbow Six Siege site and the Wikipedia article.

The three formulas that actually matter

Most of a player card reduces to three ratios.

K/D is kills / deaths, rounded to two decimals. The interesting branch is zero deaths. Returning Infinity, NaN or a blank cell makes a profile look broken. A clean rule is: if deaths are zero, return the kill count (so 12 kills and 0 deaths display as 12.00). It stays a real number you can sort.

Headshot percentage is headshots / kills. Guard the case where headshots exceed kills — that is almost always a data error, not a player feat — and do not compute a percentage from zero kills.

Win rate is where trackers quietly diverge. There are two legitimate denominators:

  • Current ranked season card: wins / (wins + losses)
  • Lifetime totals, per-mode figures and past seasons: wins / matches_played

Those two are not always equal. "Matches played" can include results that are not a clean win or loss in the ranked board you just typed in. If one site shows 61.0% and another shows 60.4% for the same account, check the denominator before you assume either is wrong.

In Python, the core is small enough to keep on one screen:

from typing import Optional

def kd(kills: int, deaths: int) -> float:
    if deaths == 0:
        return float(kills)
    return round(kills / deaths, 2)

def win_rate_season(wins: int, losses: int) -> Optional[float]:
    denom = wins + losses
    if denom == 0:
        return None  # render as a dash, not 0.0
    return round(wins / denom * 100, 1)

def win_rate_lifetime(wins: int, matches: int) -> Optional[float]:
    if matches == 0:
        return None
    return round(wins / matches * 100, 1)

Returning None (and showing a dash) when there is no sample is better than showing 0.0%, which readers will treat as a real losing record.

Where the data comes from, and how stale it is allowed to be

A tracker is not the game client. It asks a ranked-data API, caches the answer and renders a page. SiegeRadar's public description is that player profiles, operator stats, leaderboards and live player counts come from the Arenyze API, which serves Ubisoft's ranked data. The response is cached so the next view inside the window does not hit the source again.

Freshness is a product decision as much as a systems one. Refresh too often and you burn a data budget; refresh too rarely and a player who just finished a match thinks the site is broken. One working set of windows looks like this:

  • Player profiles: at most every 15 minutes
  • Operator stats: every 30 minutes (season-level operator stats every 6 hours)
  • Leaderboards: every 3 hours
  • Live player counts: every hour
  • "Player not found" misses: remembered for 10 minutes, then tried again
  • Game database pages (operators, weapons, maps, ranks): a snapshot, updated each season, not live

When the daily budget is used up, or upstream is down, serving the last saved copy with an explicit "couldn't refresh, last updated X minutes ago" is kinder than a blank page.

Other edges that will show up in bug reports

Console names must match exactly. A near miss should return "not found," not a cousin account. That feels harsh until the alternative is attaching someone else's rank to a search.

Past seasons do not share a scale. Ranked 2.0 and Ranked 3.0 use different RP ranges. Seasons before Y7S4 used MMR, not rank points, so a tracker should not invent a modern rank name for them.

Operator data is not a full career. Headshot percentage and operator time played may only cover recent seasons. Summing operator hours will usually come in under the lifetime total Ubisoft reports. Document that.

There may be no match history. Not every tracker has a replay of each lobby. If you do not have it, say so. Advertising a feature you cannot compute is worse than a shorter feature list.

Why two good trackers still disagree

Most disagreements come from four places: the win-rate denominator, the cache window, whether operator stats are treated as lifetime, and whether a missing sample is shown as zero or as empty. Get those four written down and the rest of the page is presentation. The useful test is not "does this match another site to two decimals?" It is "can I explain every number on the card, including the ones we cannot show?"

title: How to get EU public tenders from TED as JSON in Python (without learning expert-query syntax)
summary:
Every public tender above the EU thresholds, from a German city's software project to a French hospital's equipment purchase, is published in TED (Tenders Electronic Daily), the EU's official procurement journal. TED has a free, official search API. The catch is its expert query syntax, its nested multilingual fields and a single notice that can contain several lots with different deadlines and values.

This post shows a script that answers one practical question: "Which open tenders match what we sell, in the countries we serve, and are still biddable?" You get flat JSON and a CSV.

Disclosure: I built the EU Tenders (TED) API actor used below. It calls the official TED Search API v3 and only returns organisations, never contact persons.

The 20-line version 

# pip install apify-client
import csv, os
from apify_client import ApifyClient

client = ApifyClient(os.environ["APIFY_TOKEN"])

run_input = {
    "keywords": ["software"],
    "countries": ["DEU", "AUT"],      # ISO alpha-3 buyer countries
    "cpvCodes": ["72", "48"],         # IT services, software packages
    "noticeTypes": ["competition"],   # open calls for tenders
    "publishedWithinDays": 7,
    "deadlineAfter": "today",         # skip expired tenders
    "maxResults": 50,
}

run = client.actor("fast_data_asap/eu-tenders-ted-api").call(run_input=run_input)
notices = list(client.dataset(run["defaultDatasetId"]).iterate_items())

notices.sort(key=lambda n: n.get("deadline") or "9999")
fields = ["deadline", "buyerName", "buyerCity", "buyerCountry", "title", "estimatedValue", "currency", "url"]
with open("tenders.csv", "w", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    w = csv.DictWriter(f, fieldnames=fields, extrasaction="ignore")
    w.writeheader()
    w.writerows(notices)
print(len(notices), "open tenders written to tenders.csv")

No browser, no HTML parsing. The actor turns the inputs into a TED expert query, follows pagination and flattens each notice into one row.

What comes back

07.12.2026 Stadt Brandis Development of OpenCore modules for the PartheCloud €625,600
08.12.2026 BWI GmbH, Bonn Framework contract, notice "1961-JC-NoCodeDB" (software packages) not published

Every row has the same flat fields:

{
  "noticeId": "779062-2026",
  "title": "Germany – Programming services of application software – Entwicklungsleistungen für OpenCore-Module der PartheCloud",
  "buyerName": "Stadt Brandis",
  "buyerCountry": "DEU",
  "buyerCity": "Brandis",
  "cpvMain": "72212000",
  "cpvCodes": ["72212000", "72262000", "72263000"],
  "formType": "competition",
  "procedureType": "open",
  "estimatedValue": 625600,
  "currency": "EUR",
  "publishedAt": "2026-11-09",
  "deadline": "2026-12-07T12:00:00+01:00",
  "lotsCount": 1,
  "url": "https://ted.europa.eu/en/notice/-/detail/779062-2026"
}

Two details that save you work:

  • deadline is the earliest lot deadline as an ISO timestamp, so sorting and "days left" are one line.
  • estimatedValue is summed across lots. It is null when the buyer did not publish a value (BWI above), which is common.

Choosing filters that actually match your business

CPV prefixes are the most useful filter. CPV is the EU's product vocabulary, and a prefix matches everything below it:

Prefix Covers
72 IT services (consulting, development, support)
48 Software packages and information systems
79 Business services (consulting, marketing, translation)
45 Construction work
90 Cleaning, waste and environmental services
33 Medical equipment

Keywords are matched in full text in any language, so ["software", "Software", "logiciel"] widens the net across countries. Start broad, look at a week of results, then add minValueEur if small contracts are noise for you. Notices without a published value are kept, so you do not silently lose them.

Want to know who wins? Switch noticeTypes to ["result"]. Contract award notices show which buyer bought what, and often for how much: useful for competitor research and pricing.

seen_file.write_text(json.dumps(sorted(seen | {n["noticeId"] for n in new})))

for n in new:
    print(f'{n["deadline"][:10]}  {n["buyerName"]}: {n["title"][:90]}\n  {n["url"]}')

  • Titles and summaries come in the notice language. The actor prefers your language (English by default) where the notice is multilingual.
  • This is a search tool, not procurement or legal advice. Always read the official notice before bidding.

What it costs

$0.002 per notice returned, and empty runs are free. The 50-notice daily run above costs at most $0.10; a typical "last two days, two countries, two CPV codes" run returns far fewer rows.

title: Building a Resilient Offline-First Telemetry Collector in Python for Edge IoT Devices
summary:
Why Edge Devices Need Offline Resilience

When deploying IoT sensors in remote environments such as greenhouses or agricultural fields, internet connectivity is rarely guaranteed. If a sensor node fails to reach the cloud database, critical telemetry data like temperature, pH, or electrical conductivity can be permanently lost.

In this tutorial, we will build a lightweight Python telemetry collector that buffers sensor readings locally in SQLite during network outages and automatically flushes them to a remote API once connectivity is restored.

Architecture Overview

  1. Ingestion Layer: Reads incoming JSON payloads from local microcontrollers (such as an ESP32 over HTTP or MQTT).
  2. Local Buffer (SQLite): Acts as a persistent write-ahead queue when the upstream cloud endpoint is unreachable.
  3. Sync Worker: A background loop that checks network health and batches pending records to the cloud.

Setting Up the Local Buffer

First, let's create a simple SQLite schema to store unsent telemetry payloads safely on disk:

import sqlite3
import json
import time

DB_PATH = "telemetry_buffer.db"

def init_db():
    conn = sqlite3.connect(DB_PATH)
    cursor = conn.cursor()
    cursor.execute("""
        CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS pending_metrics (
            id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT,
            device_id TEXT NOT NULL,
            payload TEXT NOT NULL,
            created_at REAL NOT NULL
        )
    """)
    conn.commit()
    conn.close()

def save_locally(device_id: str, metrics: dict):
    conn = sqlite3.connect(DB_PATH)
    cursor = conn.cursor()
    cursor.execute(
        "INSERT INTO pending_metrics (device_id, payload, created_at) VALUES (?, ?, ?)",
        (device_id, json.dumps(metrics), time.time())
    )
    conn.commit()
    conn.close()

Implementing the Batch Sync Worker

Next, we create a worker function that attempts to push buffered readings to our cloud ingestion endpoint. If the request fails due to a timeout or connection error, the records remain safely stored for the next retry cycle.

import urllib.request
import urllib.error

CLOUD_ENDPOINT = "https://example.com"

def flush_buffer(batch_size: int = 50):
    conn = sqlite3.connect(DB_PATH)
    cursor = conn.cursor()
    cursor.execute(
        "SELECT id, device_id, payload, created_at FROM pending_metrics ORDER BY id ASC LIMIT ?",
        (batch_size,)
    )
    rows = cursor.fetchall()

    if not rows:
        conn.close()
        return

    batch = [
        {
            "id": row[0],
            "device_id": row[1],
            "metrics": json.loads(row[2]),
            "timestamp": row[3]
        }
        for row in rows
    ]

    try:
        req = urllib.request.Request(
            CLOUD_ENDPOINT,
            data=json.dumps({"records": batch}).encode("utf-8"),
            headers={"Content-Type": "application/json"},
            method="POST"
        )
        with urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=5) as response:
            if response.status in (200, 201):
                ids_to_delete = [(row[0],) for row in rows]
                cursor.executemany("DELETE FROM pending_metrics WHERE id = ?", ids_to_delete)
                conn.commit()
                print(f"Successfully synced {len(rows)} records.")
    except urllib.error.URLError as e:
        print(f"Network unavailable, keeping records in buffer: {e}")
    finally:
        conn.close()

Key Takeaways

  • Zero Data Loss: Using SQLite as a local queue guarantees that transient Wi-Fi drops never erase historical sensor trends.
  • Batch Efficiency: Sending 50 records in a single HTTP POST reduces TLS handshake overhead and lowers cloud API costs.
  • Idempotency: Always include the original created_at edge timestamp so backend dashboards plot metrics when they actually occurred, not when they arrived.

Next, we create a worker function that attempts to push buffered readings to our cloud ingestion endpoint. If the request fails due to a timeout or connection error, the records remain safely stored for the next retry cycle.

import urllib.error

CLOUD_ENDPOINT = "https://example.com"

def flush_buffer(batch_size: int = 50):
    conn = sqlite3.connect(DB_PATH)
    cursor = conn.cursor()
    cursor.execute(
        "SELECT id, device_id, payload, created_at FROM pending_metrics ORDER BY id ASC LIMIT ?",
        (batch_size,)
    )
    rows = cursor.fetchall()

    if not rows:
        conn.close()
        return

    batch = [
        {
            "id": row[0],
            "device_id": row[1],
            "metrics": json.loads(row[2]),
            "timestamp": row[3]
        }
        for row in rows
    ]

    try:
        req = urllib.request.Request(
            CLOUD_ENDPOINT,
            data=json.dumps({"records": batch}).encode("utf-8"),
            headers={"Content-Type": "application/json"},
            method="POST"
        )
        with urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=5) as response:

                cursor.executemany("DELETE FROM pending_metrics WHERE id = ?", ids_to_delete)

                print(f"Successfully synced {len(rows)} records.")
    except urllib.error.URLError as e:
        print(f"Network unavailable, keeping records in buffer: {e}")
    finally:

title: I built bhasha-kit: a free offline Python library for Hindi & Bengali text
summary:
Hi everyone! I'm Solo Developer. I just published my first Python package, bhasha-kit, a free, offline toolkit for Hindi, Bengali and English text.

Why I built it

Most text tools need an API key or an internet connection, and many don't handle Hindi and Bengali well. I wanted something simple that runs locally, with no dependencies.

What it does

  • Cleans text (emojis, extra spaces, Unicode)
  • Detects Hindi / Bengali / English
  • Transliterates Roman ↔ Devanagari / Bengali
  • Converts numbers to words, including rupees and paise
  • Basic sentiment analysis and keyword extraction

Install 

pip install bhasha-kit

Quick examples 

from bhasha_kit import clean_text, number_to_words, analyze_sentiment

clean_text("नमस्ते   😀 दोस्तों")
# 'नमस्ते दोस्तों'

number_to_words(1250, "hi")
# 'एक हज़ार दो सौ पचास'

number_to_words(1250, "bn")
# 'এক হাজার দুই শত পঞ্চাশ'

analyze_sentiment("this is not good")
# {'label': 'negative', 'score': -1.0, 'lang': 'en'}

  • Transliteration is rule-based and approximate.
  • Sentiment uses a small word list and doesn't understand sarcasm or context.

title: Claude for business: testing three Claude models as SQL agents on a CRM
summary:
Claude for business decisions often come down to which model to put behind an agent, and this post shows how to settle that with a small test you can rebuild on your own data: an invented CRM with known traps, ground truth computed two ways, an agent loop with one read-only SQL tool, a scorer with a tolerance, and a cost per right answer instead of a cost per token. By the end you will be able to run the same comparison on your own questions and see what a right answer costs from each model. The trigger was the launch of [Claude Fable 5.2](https://www.anthropic.com/claude-fable-and-mythos-5-2) on 9 November, at $8 / $40 per million input and output tokens, twice [the list price](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/pricing) of Opus 5.5. I had Claude Code build the test, and a GitHub workflow made the API calls. Everything below is from the real files, and every code block is trimmed from them. ![Dark cover dated 9 November 2026, kicker Claude News: Claude Fable 5.2 is here. Sonnet added up the pipeline right every time](https://brinvik.com/claude-news/2026-11-09-claude-fable-pipeline/brinvik-pipeline-cover-en-1920x1080.png) ## The setup in one paragraph Three models (Claude Fable 5.2, Claude Opus 5.5, Claude Sonnet 5.5), the same 8 questions from an invented sales director, effort medium\, 2 runs per question per condition, and two conditions: with the export's column documentation and without it. That is 32 runs per model and 96 in all. Every call, every query and every answer is written to a JSONL file. The whole thing cost $9.58 at list price. ## Building a CRM with traps on purpose pack.py\ generates an invented Danish software firm, Saltholm Data ApS, deterministically, so the same seed always gives the same database. It has 150 live deals plus 12 archived copies left over from merged duplicates, amounts in 4 currencies, 9 deals with two CFOs in the contacts table, and 16 live deals that entered proposal more than once. Each of those is there because it makes a naive total wrong. The schema the models see, trimmed to the table that matters most: \sql CREATE TABLE deals (  id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,  company\_id INTEGER REFERENCES companies(id),  owner\_id INTEGER REFERENCES users(id),  name TEXT,  pipeline TEXT,         -- 'new\_business' or 'renewal'  stage TEXT,            -- current stage: lead, qualified, proposal, negotiation, closed\_won, closed\_lost  amount REAL,           -- deal value in the deal's own currency  currency TEXT,         -- DKK, EUR, SEK or NOK  close\_date TEXT,       -- expected close date for open deals, actual close date for closed deals  archived INTEGER,      -- 1 = merged into another deal and kept for history only  merged\_into INTEGER    -- the deal this one was merged into, when archived = 1 ); \\ The other tables are deal\_contacts\ (deal, contact, role), deal\_line\_items\, stage\_history\ (deal, stage, entered_at), fx\_rates\ and users\. In the "without documentation" condition, the comments after --\ are stripped, so the model sees bare column names. ## Ground truth, computed twice truth.py\ computes the answer to every question twice: once in plain Python over the generated records, and once in SQL over the SQLite file. The script exits 1 if the two disagree by more than half a krone. For the CFO question, the SQL uses EXISTS\ so a deal with two CFOs counts once: \sql select sum(d.amount\*f.dkk\_per\_unit) from deals d join fx\_rates f on f.currency=d.currency where d.archived=0 and d.stage in ('lead','qualified','proposal','negotiation') and exists (select 1 from deal\_contacts c where c.deal\_id=d.id and c.role='CFO') \\ It also computes the naive answers, so you know what each trap would cost: DKK 12,527,857 instead of DKK 10,983,557 for the open pipeline without currency conversion (14% too big), DKK 11,772,774 with the archived copies counted (7%), and DKK 6,342,447 instead of DKK 5,083,337 when you join to contacts and sum (25%). ![Three horizontal bars on a light ground, one per trap. Each bar runs to a gold line at the true number and carries on in red: CFO rows counted twice gives 25 percent too much, currency not converted 14 percent, merged duplicates counted 7 percent](https://brinvik.com/claude-news/2026-11-09-claude-fable-pipeline/brinvik-pipeline-info-1-faelder-en-1600.jpg) ## The agent loop api\_job.py\ gives each model two tools: run\_sql\, which runs one SELECT against a read-only copy and returns at most 40 rows, and submit\_answer\, which takes the number, the SQL that produced it and a short explanation. The tool descriptions below are translated; the originals are in Danish, as is the question. \python TOOLS = \[    {"name": "run\_sql",     "description": "Run one SELECT against the CRM database (SQLite, read-only). "                    f"Returns at most {MAX\_ROWS} rows.",     "input\_schema": {"type": "object", "properties": {"sql": {"type": "string"}}, "required": \["sql"\]}},    {"name": "submit\_answer",     "description": "Submit your final answer: the number, the query that gave it and a short explanation.",     "input\_schema": {"type": "object", "properties": {         "value": {"type": "number"}, "sql": {"type": "string"}, "forklaring": {"type": "string"}},         "required": \["value", "sql", "forklaring"\]}}, \] \\ The loop is the plain tool-use loop: call the model, run every run\_sql\ it asked for, send the results back, and stop when submit\_answer\ arrives or after 14 turns. Errors are recorded, never hidden. Every one of the 96 runs ended with an answer. The connection opens the database with mode=ro\, so a model that tries an UPDATE gets an error back instead of a changed answer key. ## Scoring with a tolerance score.py\ counts an answer as right when it is within half a percent of the truth: \python right = abs(val - t) / abs(t) <= 0.005 \\ Half a percent absorbs rounding to whole kroner and tiny exchange-rate differences, and nothing else. No trap in this dataset is that small: the smallest, joining the stage history on question 5 so that a deal which entered proposal twice in October counts twice, is about 4%. The scorer also checks every wrong answer against the naive totals, so a miss is labelled with the trap that caused it, or with none. ## Cost per right answer, not per token Cost is input and output tokens times list price, with thinking counted as output. Per run, Fable 5.2 cost 18.0 cents, Opus 5.5 9.3 and Sonnet 5.5 2.7. Divide by right answers instead of runs and you get the number that matters: 2.7 cents per right answer for Sonnet, 9.3 for Opus and 19.9 for Fable, more than seven times Sonnet. Fable also used about twice Sonnet's output tokens on the same questions, and averaged 21 seconds per answer against 7. ![Three columns on a light ground, one per model, with 32 dots each. Fable 5.2 has 29 gold dots and three red rings, Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5 have 32 gold dots. Under each: 19.9, 9.3 and 2.7 cents per right answer, with a bar showing the difference](https://brinvik.com/claude-news/2026-11-09-claude-fable-pipeline/brinvik-pipeline-info-2-pris-en-1600.jpg) ## What the results were No model summed a trap in any of the 96 runs. All three left out archived copies every time and converted currency in every run that asked for kroner. Sonnet and Opus matched the answer key 32/32. Fable matched it 29/32. Fable's three misses were all question 5, "the deals that went into proposal in October". It counted only deals whose first entry into proposal was in October (17 deals, DKK 2,797,423) where the key counts every entry in October (22 deals, DKK 3,563,279). None of them was a summing trap: the SQL was correct for the reading it chose. In all 4 of its runs on that question, Fable's explanation named both readings and both numbers. Opus did it in 1 of 4, Sonnet in none. Sonnet's full marks on question 5 came from its reading matching my key. ## Taking the documentation away The counterfactual was the part I was least sure of. With the column notes stripped, Opus and Sonnet answered the same, and Fable got one more right (15/16 against 14/16), so the documentation made no difference you could measure here. Mean queries per answer went up a little: Sonnet 3.9 to 4.1, Opus 4.9 to 5.5, Fable 5.6 to 6.3. The models found archived\, the currency column and the contacts table by querying the data. The caveat is that the names were clear; a column called status\_2\ would be a different test. ## Running it without an API key in the repo The calls run in a GitHub Actions workflow that authenticates with workload identity federation, so no key exists anywhere: the client takes its identity from the workflow's federation settings, and the job only runs on the main branch by manual dispatch. verify.py\ then rebuilds the database from pack.py\, checks that the recorded copy matches it row for row, re-reads every run and writes the facts file every number in the write-up comes from. Doc set and bare set cost $4.72 and $4.86. ## Claude for business in practice: doing this on your own CRM 1. Pick five to ten questions you already know the answer to, and write the true number down before you start. 2. Give each model the schema, one read-only query tool and a submit tool that asks for the number, the SQL and an explanation. 3. Score with a tolerance, and label each miss with the trap it fell into, if any. 4. Divide cost by right answers. 5. Read the explanations, not just the numbers. That is where the ambiguous question showed up. Anthropic's own advice is to start with Opus 5.5 and move up or down as needed. On these eight questions Sonnet was as accurate as Opus at under a third of the price, so I would include Sonnet in your test; that is the advice of this one test, on invented data. The full write-up, with a demo of every run and the SQL each model wrote, is [the article testing Claude Fable 5.2 on a sales pipeline](https://brinvik.com/en/journal/claude-fable-5-2-pricing-sales-pipeline-test?utm_source=devto&utm_medium=article&utm_campaign=2026-11-09-claude-fable-pipeline&utm_content=devto-en). If you want this set up against your own CRM, that is part of my [AI advisory work for sales and RevOps teams](https://brinvik.com/en/services/ai-advisory?utm_source=devto&utm_medium=article&utm_campaign=2026-11-09-claude-fable-pipeline&utm_content=devto-service).

The script here was tested on synthetic clips (a drawn red box on a green field), not on real people.

People ask some version of this a lot: "Can I make my Bama Bound video into a GIF?" They want it for a group-chat reaction, a Discord emoji-sized loop or a forum signature. The answer is yes. The catch is that the one thing that makes the meme recognisable is a flat, saturated red banner with white capitals, and GIF is a format that only has 256 colours per frame. Get the palette wrong and the banner turns brick-orange or picks up crawling dots.

This post turns the clip into a GIF or an animated WebP and then measures what that cost: file size, frame timing, and colour error on the banner (CIE76 ΔE, roughly "how many just-noticeable steps away from the original colour"). One Python script does both.

Short answer

Output (3 s, 320 px wide, 10 fps, test clip with light grain) Size Banner ΔE Whole-frame ΔE
GIF, ffmpeg defaults (ffmpeg -i clip.mp4 out.gif) 463 KB 26.9 21.6
GIF, own palette (palettegen + paletteuse, sierra2_4a dither) 2,395 KB 1.1 1.3
GIF, own palette, no dither 2,263 KB 1.1 1.3
GIF, own palette, denoised first 1,219 KB 1.1 1.2
Animated WebP, quality 70 64 KB 3.6 2.1
  • ffmpeg's default GIF is small because it maps every frame to a fixed, generic palette. That is exactly what turns the banner red into the wrong red: ΔE 27 is a different colour, not a subtle shift.
  • Build a palette from the clip and the banner is back within about 1 ΔE (invisible). The file is five times bigger.
  • Grain is what makes GIFs huge. AI video has fine noise that changes every frame, and GIF has to store each change. Denoising first halved the size here.
  • If the place you're posting accepts animated WebP, use it. It was 37× smaller than the best GIF on this clip, with a colour error you'd need a side-by-side to see.

Why GIF struggles with this meme specifically

A GIF frame is an indexed image: up to 256 colours, and each pixel stores an index into that table. Two things follow.

  1. Which 256 colours matter. Without a custom palette, ffmpeg falls back to a general-purpose palette spread over the whole colour cube. The banner's crimson isn't in it, so every banner pixel snaps to the nearest entry, which is visibly orange-brown. Running palettegen over the actual frames puts real banner reds into the table.
  2. Dithering vs. flat areas. Error-diffusion dithering (sierra, Floyd–Steinberg) hides banding in gradients like the sky, but on a flat red area it can add a faint moving texture. Bayer (ordered) dithering adds a fixed cross-hatch. On the banner itself, "no dither" was the most accurate here. The sky looked a bit more banded, which matters less.

GIF also stores timing in hundredths of a second. 10, 20, 25 and 50 fps are exact. 12 fps isn't: ffmpeg alternates 80 ms and 90 ms delays to average out, which you can see in the script's delays_ms output. It's harmless for a reaction loop, but it's why I default to 10 fps.

The script

clip_to_gif.py encodes, then decodes the result with Pillow and compares it against the source decoded at the same times and size. Pillow handles the GIF disposal rules and animated WebP. ffmpeg 7.1's WebP decoder can't read animated WebP at all, which is a fun thing to discover at 1 a.m.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Turn a vertical banner clip into a GIF or animated WebP, then measure what it cost.

  python3 clip_to_gif.py in.mp4 out.gif  [--start 2 --duration 3 --fps 10 --width 320]
                         [--method palette|naive] [--dither sierra2_4a|bayer|none]
                         [--max-kb 4000]
  python3 clip_to_gif.py in.mp4 out.webp [--quality 70]
  add --denoise to smooth AI-video grain first (much smaller GIFs)

After encoding it decodes the result and the source at the same times and size and
reports file size, frame count, frame delays, and colour error (CIE76 delta E) on
the red banner and on the whole frame. Exit 1 if --max-kb is set and not met.
Needs ffmpeg/ffprobe on PATH, NumPy and Pillow (Pillow decodes the GIF/WebP, because
ffmpeg's WebP decoder cannot read animated WebP).
"""
import argparse, json, os, subprocess, sys
import numpy as np
from PIL import Image, ImageSequence

def run(cmd):
    subprocess.run(cmd, check=True, stdout=subprocess.DEVNULL, stderr=subprocess.PIPE)

def probe_size(path):
    out = subprocess.run(["ffprobe", "-v", "error", "-select_streams", "v:0", "-show_entries",
                          "stream=width,height", "-of", "json", path],
                         check=True, capture_output=True, text=True).stdout
    s = json.loads(out)["streams"][0]
    return s["width"], s["height"]

def frames(path, vf, w, h, n=None):
    """Decode to RGB24 frames through an optional filter chain."""
    cmd = ["ffmpeg", "-v", "error", "-i", path]
    if vf: cmd += ["-vf", vf]
    cmd += ["-f", "rawvideo", "-pix_fmt", "rgb24", "-"]
    raw = subprocess.run(cmd, check=True, capture_output=True).stdout
    a = np.frombuffer(raw, np.uint8).reshape(-1, h, w, 3)
    return a if n is None else a[:n]

def to_lab(rgb):
    c = rgb.astype(np.float64) / 255.0
    c = np.where(c <= 0.04045, c / 12.92, ((c + 0.055) / 1.055) ** 2.4)
    m = np.array([[0.4124, 0.3576, 0.1805], [0.2126, 0.7152, 0.0722], [0.0193, 0.1192, 0.9505]])
    xyz = c @ m.T / np.array([0.95047, 1.0, 1.08883])
    f = np.where(xyz > 216 / 24389, np.cbrt(xyz), (24389 / 27 * xyz + 16) / 116)
    return np.stack([116 * f[..., 1] - 16, 500 * (f[..., 0] - f[..., 1]), 200 * (f[..., 1] - f[..., 2])], -1)

def red_mask(rgb):
    """Saturated, bright, red-ish pixels: the banner, not the field or the sky."""
    c = rgb.astype(np.int16); r, g, b = c[..., 0], c[..., 1], c[..., 2]
    return (r > 120) & (r - g > 70) & (r - b > 50)

def encode(a, w_out, chain):
    if a.out.endswith(".webp"):
        run(["ffmpeg", "-v", "error", "-y", "-ss", str(a.start), "-t", str(a.duration), "-i", a.src,
             "-vf", chain, "-an", "-c:v", "libwebp_anim", "-lossless", "0", "-q:v", str(a.quality),
             "-loop", "0", a.out])
    elif a.method == "naive":
        run(["ffmpeg", "-v", "error", "-y", "-ss", str(a.start), "-t", str(a.duration), "-i", a.src,
             "-vf", chain, "-an", "-loop", "0", a.out])
    else:
        d = {"bayer": "bayer:bayer_scale=3", "none": "none"}.get(a.dither, a.dither)
        fc = (f"[0:v]{chain},split[x][y];[x]palettegen=max_colors=256:stats_mode=diff[p];"
              f"[y][p]paletteuse=dither={d}:diff_mode=rectangle")
        run(["ffmpeg", "-v", "error", "-y", "-ss", str(a.start), "-t", str(a.duration), "-i", a.src,
             "-filter_complex", fc, "-an", "-loop", "0", a.out])

def decode_anim(path):
    """Frames (RGB, after GIF disposal/WebP blending) and per-frame delays in ms."""
    im = Image.open(path); fr, delays = [], []
    for f in ImageSequence.Iterator(im):
        fr.append(np.asarray(f.convert("RGB"))); delays.append(f.info.get("duration", 0))
    return np.stack(fr), delays

def measure(a, w_out, h_out, chain):
    out_f, delays = decode_anim(a.out)
    src_f = frames(a.src, f"trim=start={a.start}:duration={a.duration},setpts=PTS-STARTPTS,{chain}",
                   w_out, h_out, len(out_f))
    n = min(len(out_f), len(src_f))
    out_f, src_f = out_f[:n], src_f[:n]
    de = np.linalg.norm(to_lab(out_f) - to_lab(src_f), axis=-1)
    m = red_mask(src_f)
    return {"file": a.out, "kb": round(os.path.getsize(a.out) / 1024, 1), "width": w_out,
            "height": h_out, "fps": a.fps, "frames": len(delays), "delays_ms": sorted(set(delays)),
            "duration_s": round(sum(delays) / 1000, 3),
            "banner_share": round(float(m.mean()), 3),
            "banner_dE_mean": round(float(de[m].mean()), 2) if m.any() else None,
            "frame_dE_mean": round(float(de.mean()), 2)}

def main():
    p = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__, formatter_class=argparse.RawDescriptionHelpFormatter)
    p.add_argument("src"); p.add_argument("out")
    p.add_argument("--start", type=float, default=0.0); p.add_argument("--duration", type=float, default=3.0)
    p.add_argument("--fps", type=int, default=10); p.add_argument("--width", type=int, default=320)
    p.add_argument("--method", choices=["palette", "naive"], default="palette")
    p.add_argument("--dither", default="sierra2_4a"); p.add_argument("--quality", type=int, default=70)
    p.add_argument("--max-kb", type=float, default=0)
    p.add_argument("--denoise", action="store_true")
    a = p.parse_args()
    if a.out.endswith(".gif") and 100 % a.fps:
        print(f"warning: GIF delays are whole 1/100 s; {a.fps} fps cannot be timed exactly "
              f"(use 10, 20, 25 or 50)", file=sys.stderr)
    while True:
        w0, h0 = probe_size(a.src)
        w_out = a.width - a.width % 2
        h_out = round(h0 * w_out / w0 / 2) * 2
        chain = f"fps={a.fps},scale={w_out}:{h_out}:flags=lanczos"
        if a.denoise: chain = "hqdn3d=8:6:12:12," + chain
        encode(a, w_out, chain)
        kb = os.path.getsize(a.out) / 1024
        if not a.max_kb or kb <= a.max_kb or a.width * 0.85 < 160:
            break
        print(f"{kb:.0f} KB at {w_out} px wide is over {a.max_kb:.0f} KB; shrinking", file=sys.stderr)
        a.width = int(a.width * 0.85)  # too big: shrink 15% and try again
    r = measure(a, w_out, h_out, chain)
    r["ok"] = not a.max_kb or r["kb"] <= a.max_kb
    print(json.dumps(r))
    return 0 if r["ok"] else 1

if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main())

The banner mask is deliberately simple: pixels where red clearly dominates green and blue. For your own clip, check banner_share. It should roughly match how much of the frame the banner fills (about 12% in my test clip). If it's near 0, the mask missed and the banner ΔE means nothing.

Test it on a clip where you know the answer

Don't tune a converter on the clip you care about. This generator draws a sky gradient, a grainy green field, and a red banner that sways left and right, with a beep track (no people, no real footage). NOISE controls how much grain the field has.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Synthetic stand-in for a vertical banner clip (no people, no real footage):
# gradient sky, noisy green field, a red banner with white text that sways
# left and right, and a soundtrack of short 880 Hz beeps at irregular times
# over a quiet 220 Hz hum.
#   ./make_field_test_clip.sh out.mp4 [WxH] [fps] [seconds]
#   env NOISE=0..40 sets the field grain (default 18)
set -euo pipefail
out=${1:-field_test.mp4}; size=${2:-480x854}; fps=${3:-30}; dur=${4:-8}
W=${size%x*}; H=${size#*x}
FONT=/usr/share/fonts/truetype/dejavu/DejaVuSans-Bold.ttf
BW=$((W*3/4)); BH=$((H/6)); BY=$((H*2/5))
BX="(${W}-${BW})/2+${W}/10*sin(2*PI*t/3.1)*cos(2*PI*t/7.3)"
SKY=$((H*2/5))
ffmpeg -v error -y \
  -f lavfi -i "gradients=s=${W}x${SKY}:c0=0x2F7FD0:c1=0xBFE3FF:x0=0:y0=0:x1=0:y1=${SKY}:r=${fps}:d=${dur}:speed=0" \
  -f lavfi -i "color=c=0x3A8A3A:s=${W}x${H}:r=${fps}:d=${dur}" \
  -f lavfi -i "color=c=0xC8102E:s=${BW}x${BH}:r=${fps}:d=${dur}" \
  -f lavfi -i "aevalsrc='0.08*sin(2*PI*220*t)+0.6*sin(2*PI*880*t)*(between(t,0.7,0.82)+between(t,2.1,2.22)+between(t,2.6,2.72)+between(t,4.9,5.02)+between(t,6.3,6.42))':s=48000:d=${dur}" \
  -filter_complex "[1:v]noise=alls=${NOISE:-18}:allf=t,format=yuv420p[field];\
[field][0:v]overlay=0:0[bg];\
[2:v]drawtext=fontfile=${FONT}:text='TEST BANNER':fontcolor=white:fontsize=$((BH/4)):x=(w-text_w)/2:y=(h-text_h)/2[ban];\
[bg][ban]overlay=x='${BX}':y=${BY},format=yuv420p[v]" \
  -map "[v]" -map 3:a -c:v libx264 -preset veryfast -crf 20 -r "$fps" -c:a aac -b:a 128k -t "$dur" "$out"
echo "wrote $out (${W}x${H} @ ${fps} fps, ${dur} s)"

Results on my box (ffmpeg 7.1, NumPy 2.5, Pillow 13), 3 seconds from 2.0 s:

$ NOISE=6 ./make_field_test_clip.sh lo.mp4
$ python3 clip_to_gif.py lo.mp4 n.gif --method naive --start 2 --duration 3
{"kb": 463.1, "frames": 30, "delays_ms": [100], "banner_dE_mean": 26.89, "frame_dE_mean": 21.59, ...}
$ python3 clip_to_gif.py lo.mp4 p.gif --start 2 --duration 3
{"kb": 2394.5, "banner_dE_mean": 1.12, "frame_dE_mean": 1.28, ...}
$ python3 clip_to_gif.py lo.mp4 pd.gif --denoise --start 2 --duration 3
{"kb": 1219.4, "banner_dE_mean": 1.08, "frame_dE_mean": 1.17, ...}
$ python3 clip_to_gif.py lo.mp4 w.webp --start 2 --duration 3
{"kb": 64.0, "banner_dE_mean": 3.59, "frame_dE_mean": 2.07, ...}
$ python3 clip_to_gif.py lo.mp4 w12.gif --fps 12 --start 2 --duration 3
warning: GIF delays are whole 1/100 s; 12 fps cannot be timed exactly (use 10, 20, 25 or 50)
{"frames": 36, "delays_ms": [80, 90], "duration_s": 3.0, ...}

With the default heavier grain (NOISE=18), the palette GIF was 3,159 KB, and denoising barely helped (3,098 KB). Past a certain amount of grain, the light hqdn3d pass can't clean it up, and you need a smaller size or a shorter loop instead.

Hitting a size limit

Many places cap GIF uploads. --max-kb re-encodes with the width shrunk by 15% each time until the file fits, then measures the final one:

$ python3 clip_to_gif.py lo.mp4 cap.gif --width 480 --fps 20 --denoise --max-kb 1500 --start 2 --duration 3
2876 KB at 480 px wide is over 1500 KB; shrinking
3637 KB at 408 px wide is over 1500 KB; shrinking
2463 KB at 346 px wide is over 1500 KB; shrinking
1757 KB at 294 px wide is over 1500 KB; shrinking
{"kb": 1313.0, "width": 248, "height": 442, "fps": 20, "banner_dE_mean": 1.27, "ok": true}

Notice that 408 px was bigger than 480 px. At 480 px the source wasn't being scaled at all. At 408 px, the Lanczos resample added fine ringing that the palette then had to dither. File size versus width isn't monotonic for GIF, so the loop checks the actual size rather than predicting it.

Choosing settings for a Bama Bound loop

  • Pick the 2–3 seconds that sell the joke, usually the banner held up and steady. The whole ~8-second clip (FAQ) is too long for a GIF.
  • Start at 320 px wide and 10 fps. Go to 20 fps only if the motion looks choppy.
  • Use your own palette, always. Try --dither none if the banner shows a crawling texture.
  • Use --denoise for grainy clips. Check the banner ΔE afterwards. It should stay under about 2.
  • Prefer animated WebP or a short MP4 wherever they're accepted. GIF is for places that accept nothing else.
  • Sound is gone in both formats. If the soundtrack is part of the joke for your audience, post the video.

Does a higher resolution help?

Not for a GIF. You're going to scale down to 320–480 px anyway, so 480p is plenty of source. The higher tiers pay off when you post the video itself on a big screen. For reference, on the pricing page today one generation is $7.98 at 480p, $9.98 at 720p, $16.98 at 1080p and $24.98 at 4k, with buyer tax added at checkout. There's no free allowance and no subscription.

One more thing: a GIF loses the context of the original post, so the person seeing it may not know it's a meme. The clip isn't an admission letter, and the University of Alabama's Bama Bound orientation is a separate, real program (about). If the loop could be taken literally, put "meme" or "AI clip" in the message you send with it.

Related: how to pick the photo (guides), what to do if a paid clip never arrived (help).
